United States.text:
As World Cup hosts, the United States get a kind start: the model has them through the group stage 87.1% of the time, top of the group at 47.7%, and into the round of 16 at 56.2%. Beyond that the picture narrows fast — a 26.9% quarter-final chance, 10.7% to reach the semis, and just 1.7% to lift the trophy on home soil. Ranked 16th by FIFA with a squad valued at €385.65m, this is a competitive side rather than a favourite, and the numbers treat the latter rounds as a steep climb.

The form line is the worry. Across their last ten, the USMNT beat Uruguay 5-1, Paraguay, Australia and Japan, but also lost 2-5 to Belgium, 0-2 to Portugal and, most recently, 1-2 at home to Germany in June. The pattern is plain: they handle teams around or below their level and get punished by the elite. A friendly schedule stacked with European heavyweights has exposed that gap, and how they fare in the knockouts will hinge on whether they can finally close it against a top-tier opponent.

Canada.text:
Canada arrive as co-hosts ranked 30th in the world, and the model likes the position that brings: a 97.7% chance of clearing the group stage into the round of 32, a 56.6% shot at winning their group, and better-than-even odds, 63.2%, of reaching the last 16. Beyond that the picture thins quickly — a quarter-final is priced at 27%, a semi-final at just 8.5%, and the title at 0.8%. With a squad valued at €198.65m, this is a team built to advance on home soil rather than to lift the trophy.

The form line is harder to read, because all ten of these matches were friendlies and nine of them were at home. Canada lost only once in that run, 0-1 to Australia, but the draws pile up: five of them, including blank stalemates against Tunisia, Ecuador and Colombia and a 2-2 with Iceland. Wins over Uzbekistan, Venezuela, Guatemala and Wales keep the record respectable, yet the recurring goalless or low-scoring finishes raise a fair question about where the goals come from once the tournament starts and the opposition stiffens.

Mexico.text:
Mexico arrive as hosts in good form, unbeaten in eight of their last ten, with the lone defeat a 1-2 to Paraguay back in November and the headline a 5-1 dismantling of Serbia in their final tune-up. That run, built largely at home, fits a side ranked 15th in the world and squares with a model that makes them clear favourites to win their group at 58 percent and gives them a 94 percent chance of clearing the round of 32. The home advantage and the friendly results both point the same way through the early rounds.

The deeper picture is more sober. Survival past the round of 16 is close to a coin flip at 57 percent, and the numbers thin out sharply after that: 24 percent to reach the quarter-finals, under 8 percent to the semis, and just 0.75 percent to lift the trophy. A squad valued at 191.85 million euros is competitive without being elite, and the model reads Mexico much as the form does — a team well placed to advance, but a genuine long shot to go all the way.

Panama.text:
Panama arrive ranked 33rd in the world, a number that flatters and constrains them in equal measure. They earned their place with conviction — a 3-0 win over El Salvador and a 3-2 result away to Guatemala in CONCACAF qualifying — and the recent friendly form holds up: a 4-2 win over the Dominican Republic, a 2-1 victory away to South Africa, and a creditable 1-1 draw with Bosnia & Herzegovina. The 2-6 loss away to Brazil is the obvious blot, a reminder of where the ceiling sits against elite opposition, but our model still gives them a 27.9 percent chance of clearing the group stage.

Beyond that, the numbers cool quickly. The ensemble puts Panama's odds of reaching the round of 16 at just 3.8 percent, the quarter-finals at 0.5 percent, and winning their group at only 1.7 percent. A squad valued at €34.55m is among the lighter in the field, and with no international goal totals listed for the named players, the attacking burden is hard to pin down. Realistically, this is a side built to compete for second place and steal a knockout berth.

Argentina.text:
Argentina arrive as reigning world champions and the model treats them accordingly, handing them a 76.3% chance to win their group and a near-certain 99.1% passage out of the round of 32. Beyond that the path narrows the way it does for everyone: 58.3% to reach the quarter-finals, 43.4% to the last four, and 18.8% to lift the trophy again. That last figure makes them one of the strongest contenders in the field, ranked third by FIFA with a squad valued at €782.5m, but it also frames the question honestly — even a champion is closer to one-in-five than a sure thing.

The form behind those numbers is hard to argue with. Argentina have won eight of their last ten, including a 6-0 demolition of Puerto Rico and a 5-0 of Zambia, with the only blemishes a 1-1 draw against Colombia and a 0-1 loss away to Ecuador in qualifying. Recent friendlies against Honduras, Mauritania and Angola all went their way without conceding much, suggesting a team arriving in rhythm rather than searching for it.

Brazil.text:
Brazil arrive ranked sixth in the world and carrying the most expensive squad in the field at €928.2m, yet the model is more measured than the badge suggests. It gives them a 61.3% chance of winning their group and a comfortable 98.3% to clear the round of 32, but the path narrows fast: 48.3% to reach the quarter-finals, 31% to the semis, and just 10.1% to lift the trophy. That makes them genuine contenders rather than runaway favourites, and the steep drop after the last eight is where this campaign will be decided.

The recent form reads like a side still settling. Brazil closed their warm-ups with wins over Egypt (2-1), a 6-2 rout of Panama and a 3-1 over Croatia, but the body of work is uneven — a 1-2 home loss to France in March and, more worryingly, a 0-1 qualifying defeat away to Bolivia and a 2-3 loss in Japan. The goalkeeping depth is real, with Alisson, Ederson and Weverton all in the picture, and the back line is experienced. The talent is there; the consistency, on this evidence, is the open question.

Colombia.text:
Colombia arrive ranked 13th in the world and carrying form that backs it up. Los Cafeteros closed their warm-up schedule with wins over Jordan (2-0) and Costa Rica (3-1), and their qualifying punch is clear from a 6-3 demolition of Venezuela and a 3-0 home win over Bolivia. The only blemishes recently came against serious European company, March defeats to France (1-3) and Croatia (1-2) at home, a reminder that the step up in class is real. With a squad valued at €302m and an experienced spine in goal and defence, this is a side built to go deep rather than just turn up.

The model reads them as genuine contenders without quite making them favourites. It gives Colombia a 34.8% chance of winning their group, 86.9% to clear the round of 32 and 56.4% to reach the last 16, but the odds thin quickly after that: 29.9% to make the quarters, 14.8% the semis, and just 6.9% to reach the final. A 3.0% title chance puts them firmly in the second tier of hopefuls, dangerous to anyone but short of the elite.

Uruguay.text:
Marcelo Bielsa's Uruguay arrive ranked 17th in the world and carrying a squad worth €359.3m, but recent form muddies the picture. The qualifying body of work was solid enough — a 3-0 win over Peru, 2-0 over Venezuela, a goalless draw in Chile — yet the friendly run since has been uneven. Creditable away draws against England (1-1) and Algeria (0-0) sit beside a chastening 1-5 defeat in the USA and a blank against Mexico. For a side built around defenders like Araújo and Giménez, the leaking of five goals in a single night is the kind of result that lingers.

The model treats them as a strong but not elite outfit. Reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 90.6%, and there's a 37.2% chance of surviving to the last 16, but the odds thin quickly after that: 21.2% to reach the quarters, 10.8% the semis, and just 1.9% to lift the trophy. Winning their group is rated only 22.6%, so a tougher knockout path looks the likelier route — and on that road, the back line's recent wobbles matter.

Ecuador.text:
Ecuador arrive unbeaten across their last ten, a run that says less about firepower than about how hard they are to break down: four wins and six draws, with 0-0s against Paraguay and Canada, 1-1 stalemates with the Netherlands and Morocco, and a 1-0 home win over Argentina in qualifying. That defensive backbone is where the €368.7m squad value concentrates, in names like Pacho, Hincapié, Ordoñez and Estupiñán. The recent friendly wins over Guatemala (3-0) and Saudi Arabia (2-1) hint at a sharper edge, but the pattern of low-scoring draws is the truer signal for a side ranked 23rd in the world.

The model treats them as a solid knockout team rather than a contender. It gives La Tricolor an 89.6% chance of clearing the group stage and 48.9% of reaching the last 16, essentially a coin flip, before the odds thin to 21.6% for the quarters and just 1.5% to lift the trophy. Winning their group sits at 28.2%, so a runners-up route looks the likelier path. Grind out results, and the round of 16 is genuinely within reach.

Paraguay.text:
Paraguay arrive ranked 40th in the world, a side whose pedigree — ten World Cup appearances, a quarter-final in 2010 and two Copa América titles — outstrips a fairly modest squad value of €153.65m. The form is genuinely mixed. La Albirroja closed their South American qualifying campaign solidly enough, a 1-0 win in Peru and a goalless draw at home to Ecuador either side of a narrow loss in Brazil, but the friendly run since has wobbled, with defeats to the USA, South Korea and Morocco offset by wins over Mexico and Greece and a thumping 4-0 over Nicaragua in June. The defence, built around Alderete, Balbuena and Gómez, is the recognisable backbone.

The model treats them as a side likely to survive but unlikely to surge. It gives Paraguay a 52.9% chance of getting out of the expanded group stage but only 11.98% to win the group outright, and the odds thin sharply from there: 20.7% to reach the last 16, 5.6% to the quarter-finals, and just 0.08% to lift the trophy. A team to respect defensively, not one the numbers expect to run deep.

Germany.text:
Germany arrive in form. Nine wins from their last ten leaves only a 0-2 defeat at Slovakia in September 2025 as a blemish, and they avenged it emphatically with a 6-0 thrashing in November. The qualifying run was ruthless — four clean sheets, double-digit goals across the Luxembourg and Northern Ireland fixtures — and the friendlies kept the momentum going, with a 4-0 dismissal of Finland and a 2-1 win away to the USA in early June. Ranked tenth by FIFA and carrying a squad valued at €947m, this is a side built to go deep.

The model, though, is more measured than the results sheet suggests. Germany are near-certain to clear the group stage at 96.2%, but only 48.9% to actually win their group, and the odds thin quickly after that: 30.2% to reach the quarter-finals, 15.2% for the semis, and just 2.8% to lift the trophy. That gap between glittering form and a cautious title number is the honest tension here — a team good enough to beat anyone on the day, but not yet priced as a favourite to win seven straight.

England.text:
England arrive ranked fourth in the world and qualified for the World Cup the hard way only on paper: their European campaign was a clean sweep, including 5-0 wins away in Latvia and Serbia, plus 2-0 results over Serbia at home and Albania away. The warm-up form is the wobble. A 1-0 win over New Zealand in June bookends a patchy spring that featured a 0-1 home loss to Japan and a 1-1 draw with Uruguay, and the year before saw a 1-3 home defeat to Senegal. Against ranked opposition this side has not always convinced.

The model still likes them. A squad valued at €1.36bn carries a 74.1% chance of winning the group and a near-certain 98.6% to clear the round of 32, though the path narrows fast: 50.9% to reach the quarter-finals and 31.0% to the semis. Lifting the trophy sits at 10.5%, with a final appearance at 18.0%. That makes England a genuine contender rather than a favourite — strong enough to go deep, not yet proven enough to bank on.

France.text:
France arrive at the 2026 World Cup as the world's number one ranked side, and the squad's €1.52bn valuation tells you why they sit among the favourites. Our model makes them 56.2% to win their group and gives them a 96% chance of reaching the last 32, with the path narrowing sensibly from there: 72.3% to make the round of 16, 46.1% to reach the quarter-finals, and 8.3% to lift the trophy. That champion number is the headline — Les Bleus are firmly in the contender bracket without being runaway favourites.

The recent form is solid rather than flawless. Their qualifying campaign was strong, including a 4-0 dismantling of Ukraine and a comfortable 2-0 away win over the same side, with only a 2-2 draw in Iceland to blot it. Spring friendlies brought eye-catching away wins over Brazil (2-1) and Colombia (3-1), proof they can handle quality. But the 1-2 home loss to Ivory Coast in June is a reminder that this is not an invincible team. With Maignan behind a defence built around Konaté and the Hernández brothers, the foundations look right for a deep run.

Spain.text:
Ranked second in the world and carrying a squad valued at €1.22bn, Spain arrive as one of the genuine contenders, and the model agrees: a 14.2% title chance is among the shortest in the field, with a 24.2% shot at reaching the final and a 50.4% chance of seeing out the quarter-finals. Winning their group is treated as the likely outcome at 74.8%, and survival to the last 32 is all but assumed at 99.2%. This is the profile of a team expected to go deep rather than merely turn up.

The form behind those numbers is split. European qualifying was emphatic — six wins including 6-0 away to Türkiye, 4-0 against both Georgia and Bulgaria, before a 2-2 home draw with Türkiye took the gloss off. The spring and summer friendlies have been flatter still: a goalless draw with Egypt and a 1-1 against Iraq sit awkwardly beside the 3-1 win over Peru and 3-0 over Serbia. The model still rates them a championship-class side, but the recent stutters are a fair reason to keep that 14.2% honest rather than treat the title as anything close to settled.

Portugal.text:
Roberto Martínez's Portugal arrive ranked fifth in the world with a squad valued at just over a billion euros, and the model treats them as genuine contenders without quite installing them as favourites. It gives them a 53.7% chance of winning their group and a 69.2% chance of reaching the last 16, but the odds thin quickly thereafter: 44% to make the quarter-finals, 13.1% to reach the final and 6.7% to lift the trophy. That is the profile of a strong side expected to go deep rather than one tipped to win outright.

The recent form explains both the optimism and the caveats. Portugal closed qualification by hammering Armenia 9-1 and have since won friendlies against Chile and the USA, with a goalless draw in Mexico in between. But the 0-2 loss away to the Republic of Ireland and the 2-2 home draw with Hungary are the kind of stumbles that keep the champion number down at single figures. With Cristiano Ronaldo captaining a defence built around Rúben Dias and Diogo Costa, the talent is obvious; turning a 6.7% chance into more is the open question.

Netherlands.text:
The Netherlands arrive seventh in the world and carrying a €754.2m squad built on a familiar defensive spine — Van Dijk, Aké, Dumfries and Timber in front of a three-man goalkeeping rotation of Flekken, Roefs and Verbruggen. Their qualifying campaign did the job without ever looking imperious: four 4-0 wins over Lithuania, Finland and Malta sat alongside two 1-1 draws with Poland, the kind of record that gets you to a World Cup but leaves questions about the very top end.

The model reads them as a solid second-tier contender rather than a favourite. It gives them a 90.1% chance of clearing the opening round and a 43.1% shot at winning their group, but the odds thin quickly after that — 42.0% to reach the last 16, 25.2% to make the quarters, and just 2.4% to lift the trophy. Recent friendlies offer little reassurance: a 0-1 home loss to Algeria and a 1-1 draw with Ecuador in spring, sandwiching narrow wins over Uzbekistan and Norway. The pieces are clearly there; the form, for now, is asking to be convinced.

Belgium.text:
Belgium arrive ranked ninth in the world and carrying the form to match: their last ten games include a 5-0 demolition of Tunisia, a 2-0 win away to Croatia and a string of heavy qualifying victories, among them 7-0 over Liechtenstein and 6-0 against Kazakhstan. The blemishes are the draws — 1-1 in Kazakhstan, 0-0 at home to FYR Macedonia and 1-1 in Mexico — which suggest a side that crushes weaker opponents but can be frustrated by organised ones. With a squad valued at €547.5m and Thibaut Courtois behind a back line built around Castagne, Debast and Mechele, the platform is there.

The model makes them clear favourites to win their group at 63 percent, and reaching the last 32 is close to a formality at 94 percent. Beyond that the path narrows quickly: a 66 percent shot at the round of 16, but only 36 percent to reach the quarter-finals and 16 percent to make the semis. The title number is a sober 2.9 percent — Belgium look a safe bet to advance, but not yet a credible one to lift the trophy.

Austria.text:
Austria arrive in good rhythm, with a qualifying campaign that read mostly green: wins over Bosnia & Herzegovina away, Cyprus home and away, and a pair of double-digit-friendly demolitions of San Marino, the only blemishes a 1-1 home draw with Bosnia and a narrow 0-1 loss in Romania. The three pre-tournament friendlies all ended in wins, including a 5-1 rout of Ghana, so a team ranked 24th in the world comes in settled rather than searching. A squad valued at €242.2m leans on an experienced defensive spine, with David Alaba, Kevin Danso and Maximilian Friedl anchoring the back line.

The model treats them as a solid second-tier side rather than a contender. It gives Austria a 70.7% chance of clearing the round of 32 and 21.2% of reaching the last 16, but the numbers thin quickly after that: 8.3% to make the quarter-finals and just 2.4% to a semi. Winning the group is priced at only 7.9%, and the title at a token 0.15%. The honest read is a team good enough to advance and capable of a knockout scare, but no further.

Switzerland.text:
Switzerland arrive ranked 19th in the world and built on a settled, defensively solid spine — Manchester City's Manuel Akanji anchors a back line in a squad valued at €332.5m. Their qualifying campaign was the real evidence: 4-0 over Kosovo, 3-0 against Slovenia, and a home-and-away double over Sweden including a 4-1 win, dropping points only in two draws away to Slovenia and Kosovo. The friendlies since have been patchier — a 4-1 win over Jordan but also a 3-4 home defeat to Germany and recent draws with Norway and Australia — so the form heading in is steady rather than soaring.

The model reads them as a team almost certain to escape the first stage: 95.6% to reach the round of 32 and a 39.7% chance of topping their group. From there the picture cools quickly, as it does for most sides of this tier — 55.7% to make the round of 16, 20.2% to reach the quarter-finals, and just 0.7% to win the whole thing. That profile fits a well-organised side likely to go deep enough to matter, without the ceiling of a genuine favourite.

Turkey.text:
Turkey arrive in good form, winning eight of their last ten and going unbeaten across their final stretch of European qualifying, including a 2-2 draw away to Spain in November. The blot on that record is glaring, though: a 0-6 home defeat to the same Spain side in September, the kind of result that shows how quickly things can unravel against elite opposition. Ranked 22nd in the world with a squad valued at €473.7m, this is a team that brushes aside the likes of Bulgaria 6-1 and Georgia 4-1, but the gap to the top tier remains real.

The model sees Turkey as solid rather than special. They are roughly a coin-flip to win their group at 19.3%, with a 64.7% chance of clearing the round of 32 and a 30.0% shot at reaching the last 16. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast: 9.4% to make the quarter-finals, 2.7% for the semis, and just 0.17% to lift the trophy. That feels about right for a side capable of beating anyone on its day and losing heavily on its worst.

Croatia.text:
Croatia arrive ranked 11th in the world and carrying a squad worth €387.3m, and their European qualifying campaign backed up that pedigree: six wins from the run shown here, including a 4-0 and a 3-2 over Montenegro, a 3-0 against Gibraltar and a goalless draw away in the Czech Republic. The warm-up friendlies told a more mixed story, with wins over Slovenia (2-1) and Colombia (2-1) sitting alongside home and away defeats to Belgium (0-2) and Brazil (1-3). The defensive core, built around Gvardiol, Stanisic and Pongracic, looks the strength.

The model treats them as a solid second-tier side rather than a contender. It makes Croatia 87.2% to clear the round of 32 and gives them just a 20.5% chance of topping their group, with the real test arriving at the round of 16, which it has them surviving only 38.8% of the time. From there the odds thin quickly: 14.7% to reach the quarters, 5.8% a semi-final, and only 0.6% to lift the trophy. A capable knockout team, in short, but not one the numbers expect to go deep.

Scotland.text:
Scotland arrive ranked 43rd in the world with a squad valued at €170.25m, and the run-in suggests a team that peaks when the stakes are real. The qualifying campaign was the proof: a 4-2 win over Denmark in November, a 3-1 home thrashing of Greece, and a 0-0 draw away in Copenhagen showed both bite and resilience. The friendlies since have been a mixed bag — back-to-back home defeats to Japan and Ivory Coast in March, both 0-1, before 4-0 and 4-1 wins over Bolivia and Curaçao restored the goal flow. That's a side that beats who it should and stumbles against the better names.

The model frames this as a knockout-or-bust trip. It gives Scotland a 42.9% chance of reaching the round of 32 and just 10.5% of seeing the last 16, with winning the group a distant 2.9%. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast — 2.5% to the quarters, and a champion's price barely registering at 0.01%. The realistic target is survival into the knockouts, and on qualifying form that's a coin-flip worth backing.

Morocco.text:
Morocco arrive ranked eighth in the world and in the kind of form that backs the number up. The Atlas Lions have lost none of their last ten, winning their Africa Cup of Nations campaign with five straight clean-sheet victories — including a 3-0 win away to Senegal and a goalless draw at Nigeria — before piling up friendly wins over Burundi (5-0) and Madagascar (4-0). The only recent blemishes are home draws against Ecuador and Norway, both 1-1. With a squad valued at €498.3m and a defensive spine of Hakimi, Aguerd and Bounou, this is a side built to frustrate and counter, and the run suggests the back line is the foundation.

The model likes them without quite making them favourites. It gives Morocco a 94.3% chance of clearing the group of 32 and a 34.4% shot at winning their group, but the path narrows quickly: 56.6% to reach the last 16, 36.4% to the quarter-finals, and just 4.9% to lift the trophy. That champion number puts them in the contender bracket rather than the front rank — a deep run is the realistic ceiling, and anything beyond the quarters would beat the projection.

Senegal.text:
Ranked 14th in the world and carrying a squad valued at €478.1m, Senegal arrive as one of CAF's heavyweights, and their recent record backs that up. The Lions de la Teranga ran deep at the Africa Cup of Nations, beating Botswana, Benin, Sudan, Mali and Egypt before a 3-0 loss to Morocco ended the run. Friendly form since has been mixed: a 2-0 win over Peru and a 3-1 win over Gambia in March, then a 2-3 defeat to the USA at the end of May. The spine is experienced, anchored by defenders Kalidou Koulibaly and Moussa Niakhaté and a goalkeeping group that includes Édouard Mendy.

The model treats them as a solid knockout side rather than a favourite. It gives Senegal an 83.7% chance to clear the group stage and a 46.7% shot at the round of 16, but the odds thin quickly after that — 21.4% to reach the quarter-finals, 9.4% to make the semis, and just 1.4% to lift the trophy. Winning their group is rated at 22.5%, so the early draws look genuinely competitive.

Egypt.text:
Ranked 29th in the world with a squad valued at €116.48m, Egypt arrive carrying the familiar shape of a side that defends well and scores in small margins. The recent form reads as a team in transition: a tidy 1-0 friendly win over Russia in May, a goalless draw away to Spain in March and a 4-0 dismantling of Saudi Arabia point to genuine ceiling, but the Africa Cup of Nations told a harder story, with the run ending in defeats to Senegal and Nigeria after early wins over Benin and Ivory Coast. The Pharaohs were beaten 1-2 by Brazil in their last outing.

The model treats them as solid but not dangerous. It gives Egypt a 68.1% chance of clearing the group stage and reaching the round of 32, but only 27.3% to make the last 16 and 15.4% to actually win their group. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast — 7.5% to reach the quarter-finals, 2% a semi-final, and just a 0.1% shot at the title. This is a team built to survive the opening hurdle, with everything after that an uphill climb.

Ivory Coast.text:
The Elephants arrive in good order. The reigning African champions — their third continental title came in 2023 — have been busy beating proper opposition, edging France 2-1 and Scotland 1-0 away, and thumping South Korea 4-0, all on the road. Ranked 34th by FIFA and carrying a squad worth €522.1m, this is a side built on defensive talent, with Kossounou, Diomande and Agbadou anchoring a back line and three goalkeepers in Fofana, Koné and Lafont fighting for the gloves.

The model likes them to advance but not much more. It gives Ivory Coast an 85.8% chance of clearing the round of 32 and a 41.6% shot at the last 16, but only a 22.3% chance of actually winning their group — a coin-toss-and-then-some that frames the opening matches as the real test. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast: 16.2% to reach the quarter-finals, 6.2% to the semis, and just 0.71% to lift the trophy. A strong recent run and a settled defence make the knockout rounds a realistic target; the deeper stages remain a long shot.

South Africa.text:
Bafana Bafana arrive at the World Cup ranked 60th in the world and carrying one of the more modest squads in the field, valued at just €49.25m. Recent form does little to inspire: South Africa have won only one of their last six, a run that includes a 1-2 home defeat to Cameroon that ended their Africa Cup of Nations, draws with Nicaragua and Jamaica, and a home loss to Panama. The goals have dried up too — four straight matches without a multi-goal return tells you plenty about an attack still searching for a reliable edge.

The model treats them as long shots and the numbers are blunt about it. South Africa are given just a 4.15% chance of winning their group and a 33.96% shot at surviving into the round of 32, which makes the knockouts more likely than not to end early. From there it falls away fast: 7.26% to reach the last 16, 1.14% to the quarter-finals, and effectively nothing beyond that. Getting out of the group at all would count as a real achievement for this side.

DR Congo.text:
The Leopards arrive in North America the hard way, having edged Jamaica 1-0 in the intercontinental play-off to seal their place. That capped a strong stretch: away results at Cameroon and Nigeria during African qualifying, a run to the Africa Cup of Nations that included a 3-0 win at Botswana and a draw with Senegal, and a goalless friendly with Denmark in June. Ranked 46th by FIFA with a squad valued at €143.9m, DR Congo travel as outsiders but not pushovers, and the goalkeeping depth of Epolo, Fayulu and Mpasi underlines a team built to defend.

The model frames the realistic ceiling clearly. It gives DR Congo a 41.1% chance of getting out of the group into the round of 32, but only 12.4% to reach the last 16 and 5.4% to win their group outright, so survival looks more like a coin-flip than a comfortable expectation. Beyond that the numbers thin fast: 3.4% to reach a quarter-final, and just 0.04% to lift the trophy. A knockout berth is the sensible target, and the model treats it as genuinely in the balance.

Tunisia.text:
The Eagles of Carthage arrive ranked 44th in the world, one of seven World Cup appearances in their history, but the form line heading in is a worry. Their two final warm-ups brought a 0-1 defeat in Austria and a 0-5 thrashing in Belgium, and across the last four friendlies Tunisia have managed a single goal — a 1-0 win over Haiti — alongside a goalless draw with Canada. The Africa Cup of Nations earlier in the season was equally uneven: a 3-1 win over Uganda, but a 3-2 loss to Nigeria and draws with Tanzania and Mali that left little momentum.

The model treats them as outsiders, and the numbers back that up. A €69.95m squad is among the lighter at the tournament, and Tunisia are given just a 5.25% chance of winning their group and a 39.1% shot at surviving to the round of 32. Beyond that the path narrows fast — 8.9% to reach the last 16, 2.45% to the quarter-finals. On recent evidence, finding goals will decide whether they outrun those odds.

Japan.text:
Japan arrive in form that demands attention: their last ten reads like a statement, with 1-0 away wins over England and Scotland in March, a 3-0 dismissal of Bolivia, and a 3-2 friendly defeat of Brazil last October. The blemishes are minor and old — a 0-2 loss in the USA and a goalless draw in Mexico back in September — and the recent run of three straight 1-0 wins points to a side that defends a lead well. Ranked 18th in the world, with a squad valued at €270.85m, this is a tournament-hardened group built around defenders like Itakura, Ito and the veteran Nagatomo.

The model likes them to advance but stops short of treating them as contenders. It gives Japan a 43.4% chance to win their group and a 90.2% chance to reach the round of 32, but the path narrows quickly: 43.1% to make the last 16, 26.5% to reach the quarter-finals, and just 2.8% to lift the trophy. That is the profile of a solid, well-organised side likely to escape its group, with the deeper knockout rounds a genuine open question rather than an expectation.

South Korea.text:
South Korea arrive 25th in the world and valued at a modest €139m, and their recent form reads like a team that flatters and frustrates in equal measure. The last ten friendlies split sharply: comfortable wins over the USA (2-0 away), Paraguay, Bolivia and Ghana, plus a 5-0 demolition of Trinidad and Tobago, sit alongside heavy defeats by the genuine heavyweights — 0-5 to Brazil and 0-4 to Ivory Coast. Against that backdrop the recent 1-0 win over El Salvador and a 2-2 draw away to Mexico look like the honest middle. This is a side that handles its level and gets punished above it.

The model reflects exactly that. South Korea are favoured to clear the group stage, with an 81 percent chance of reaching the round of 32, but the odds thin quickly thereafter: 36 percent to make the last 16, 11 percent to reach the quarter-finals, and just 3 percent to go further into the semis. Winning the group is rated at 26 percent, and the title is a distant 0.2 percent. A solid knockout berth looks the realistic ceiling here.

Iran.text:
Iran arrive ranked 21st in the world and in decent touch, with three friendly wins on the spin including a 5-0 thumping of Costa Rica away and a 2-0 home win over Mali in June. The deeper run, though, was choppier: defeats to Russia and Nigeria, a 1-2 loss to Uzbekistan at home in the CAFA Nations Cup and a draw with Tajikistan suggest a side that can carve up modest opposition but stalls against organised, motivated teams. The squad is goalkeeper-heavy on paper — Beiranvand, Hosseini and Niazmand all listed — and valued at just €32.05m, modest for this stage.

The model reads them as a team built to survive rather than surge. It gives Iran a 66.7% chance of clearing the group into the round of 32, but only 25.7% to reach the last 16 and 6.8% to make a quarter-final. Winning the group is priced at 15.3%, and anything beyond the last eight drops off a cliff — 1.7% for a semi-final, 0.08% to lift the trophy. A grind-it-out campaign with a real but narrow knockout window.

Australia.text:
Australia arrive ranked 27th in the world with a modestly valued squad at €77.45m, and a recent record that pulls in two directions. The Socceroos closed their FIFA Series in March with real authority — a 1-0 win over Cameroon and a 5-1 demolition of Curaçao — but the wider picture is patchier, with four defeats in their last ten, including limp scorelines away to Colombia (0-3), Venezuela (0-1) and Mexico (0-1). The most recent outing, a 1-1 draw in Switzerland, reads as a respectable benchmark against stronger opposition.

The model treats them as a credible but not dangerous knockout side. It gives Australia a 68.8% chance of escaping the group stage at the round-of-32 cut, but only a 33.6% shot at reaching the last 16 and an 11.5% chance of a quarter-final. Winning the group is rated at 21%, while the deep runs thin out fast — 3.7% to a semi-final and just 0.3% to lift the trophy. In short, the numbers frame a team likely to feature into the second week, with little expectation beyond it.

Saudi Arabia.text:
Saudi Arabia arrive at this World Cup ranked 61st in the world and carrying one of the lighter squads in the field, valued at just €40.68m. The recent form does little to inspire: the 3-0 friendly win over Puerto Rico in June was a welcome lift, but it followed back-to-back defeats to Ecuador and Serbia, a 0-4 home thrashing by Egypt, and a patchy Arab Cup that ended with losses to Morocco and Jordan. The defence has leaked freely, and with no listed international goals among the named players, the goal threat looks an open question.

The model is unsentimental about it. It gives the Green Falcons a 30.7% chance of escaping the group into the round of 32, but only a 1.3% shot at winning their group outright. Beyond that the road narrows sharply: 4.1% to reach the last 16, 0.8% to the quarter-finals, and effectively no path to the title. This is a squad the numbers frame as an outsider hoping to spring a single result rather than build a run, and the recent results give little reason to argue the model is being harsh.

Uzbekistan.text:
Uzbekistan arrive ranked 50th in the world, an AFC side with a squad valued at €85.33m, and the model treats them as clear outsiders. It gives them a 43.9% chance of clearing the round of 32 — essentially a coin flip to get out of the opening stage — but only 14.1% to reach the round of 16 and 3.9% to make the quarter-finals. Winning their group is priced at 6.1%, and the deep-run numbers fade fast from there, down to 0.04% to lift the trophy. This is a team the model expects to be competitive early and then stretched.

The recent form reads as honest preparation rather than alarm. Through late 2025 they strung together wins over Kuwait, Egypt and Gabon plus goalless draws against Iran and Venezuela, but the June friendlies told a harder story: 0-2 away to Canada and 1-2 away to the Netherlands, both losses against stronger opposition. That gap is the question the model is pricing — solid against mid-tier sides, second-best against the elite. Whether Uzbekistan's group draw leans toward the former or the latter will decide their tournament.

Jordan.text:
Jordan arrive at their first World Cup ranked 63rd in the world with a squad valued at just €20.3m, modest numbers that the model reflects without much sympathy. It gives Al Nashama a 14.3% chance of escaping the group into the round of 32, only a 1.6% shot at the last 16, and barely 0.6% to win the group outright. Champion odds round to zero. This is a side the simulations treat as an outsider doing well simply to survive the opening round.

The form line tells a split story. December's Arab Cup run was genuinely impressive — five wins on the bounce, including 3-0 away at Egypt and 1-0 results away to Saudi Arabia and at home to Iraq, before a 2-3 loss to Morocco. But 2026 has been harder going: two draws at home against Costa Rica and Nigeria, then back-to-back defeats away to Switzerland, 1-4, and Colombia, 0-2. Against stronger opposition the goals have dried up at one end and leaked at the other, which is roughly why the model keeps Jordan's ceiling so low.

Qatar.text:
Qatar arrive ranked 55th in the world and carrying a squad valued at just €19.93m, and the recent form does little to lift the mood. The Maroons have won only once in their last ten — a 2-1 home defeat of the United Arab Emirates in October qualifying — while drawing four and losing five, including heavy beatings by Tunisia (0-3) and Russia (1-4) and a chastening 1-2 loss at home to Zimbabwe. A goalless friendly draw with El Salvador in June was the most recent outing, and goals have been scarce throughout that run.

The model reflects that struggle. It gives Qatar a 23.3% chance of surviving to the round of 32 but only 2.84% of reaching the round of 16, and the path narrows sharply from there: 0.27% to the quarter-finals and effectively nothing beyond. Winning the group is priced at a slim 1.18%. None of this is a death sentence — a single result can swing a 23% survival shot — but on present evidence Qatar look more likely to make up the numbers than to spring a surprise.

New Zealand.text:
New Zealand arrive as one of the tournament's makeweights, ranked 85th in the world with a squad valued at just €34.35m, and the form line does little to lift the mood. The last ten games yielded a single win — a 4-1 demolition of Chile in March — alongside a lone draw against Norway and eight defeats, including a 0-4 thrashing by Haiti and a 0-1 loss to England in the most recent friendlies. Back-to-back losses to Australia bookend a run that reads as a team comfortable against weaker opposition but routinely outclassed above its level.

The model sees roughly that. It gives New Zealand a 40.8% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32, but the odds thin sharply after that: 10.8% to reach the last 16, under 2% to make a quarter-final, and effectively zero to win the thing. Winning the group is a 6.4% long shot. With three goalkeepers and five defenders among the named men — Tyler Bindon and Michael Boxall anchoring the back line — this looks like a side built to stay compact and hope to nick a result rather than chase one.

Norway.text:
Norway arrive ranked 31st in the world, back on the big stage after a qualifying campaign that did its talking with goals. The run that mattered included an 11-1 demolition of Moldova, a 5-0 of Israel, and back-to-back 4-1 wins over Estonia and away to Italy in November — the kind of scoring that explains why Ståle Solbakken's side, valued at 589.9m euros, travel with genuine ambition rather than just relief at being here. The recent friendlies have been cooler: a 3-1 win over Sweden but also a 1-1 draw with Morocco, a goalless stalemate against Switzerland and a 1-2 loss in the Netherlands.

The model reads them as a solid knockout side rather than a contender. It gives Norway an 81.2% chance to clear the first round and a 43.4% shot at the round of 16, but only a 20.3% chance of winning their group and 18.9% of reaching the quarter-finals. Beyond that the numbers thin quickly — 7.7% to a semi-final, 0.9% to lift the trophy. A team that can blow weaker opponents away, then, but one the model expects to meet its ceiling in the second week.

Sweden.text:
Sweden arrive ranked 38th in the world with a squad worth €406m, but the form line reads like a warning. Their World Cup qualifying campaign was grim — beaten by Kosovo home and away, thrashed 4-1 and 2-0 by Switzerland, and held by Slovenia twice — before late wins over Ukraine and Poland steadied things. The recent friendlies offered little comfort either: a 1-3 loss to Norway and a 2-2 draw with Greece. This is a side built around defenders, with Lindelöf, Hien, Lagerbielke and Ekdal anchoring a backline that has too often leaked goals.

The model is unconvinced and the numbers explain why. It gives Sweden just a 49.9% chance of clearing the group stage — essentially a coin flip — and only 8.3% to win their group. Beyond that the path narrows sharply: 12.7% to reach the last 16, 4% to the quarter-finals, and a barely-there 0.06% to lift the trophy. For a nation with this defensive pedigree the floor should be solid, but on recent evidence even surviving the group is a genuinely open question rather than a formality.

Czech Republic.text:
The Czech Republic arrive ranked 41st in the world, and their recent form reads better than that number suggests: nine of their last ten matches without defeat, the only blemish a 1-2 loss away to the Faroe Islands back in October. Qualifying produced draws against Croatia, Denmark and Ireland alongside a 6-0 demolition of Gibraltar, and warm-up wins over Kosovo and Guatemala kept the momentum going into the summer. A squad valued at €188.18m, built around experienced defenders like Vladimír Coufal and Tomáš Holeš, is solid rather than spectacular.

Our model treats them as a side likely to survive the opening stage but unlikely to go deep. It gives them a 60.85% chance of reaching the round of 32 and just 11.73% to win their group, with the odds tightening fast thereafter: 19.44% to make the last 16, 4.24% to reach the quarter-finals, and effectively nothing — 0.01% — to lift the trophy. That profile fits a team capable of grinding out results, as the goalless draw with Croatia showed, without the firepower to threaten the tournament's heavyweights.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.text:
Bosnia and Herzegovina arrive ranked 65th in the world and worth €151.6m, a squad that ground out results rather than blowing teams away in qualifying. The recent form line is heavy on draws — 1-1 against Italy and Wales, 0-0 with FYR Macedonia, 1-1 with Panama — punctuated by sharper wins like 3-1 over Romania and 6-0 at San Marino. That profile, a team that rarely loses but only occasionally converts dominance into goals, fits a side built from the back. Kolasinac, Dedic and Katic anchor a defender-heavy core, with three goalkeepers in Jurkas, Vasilj and Zlomislic competing for the gloves.

The model treats this as a side likely to feature but unlikely to linger. It gives Bosnia just a 2.6% shot at winning their group and a 40.6% chance of surviving to the round of 32 — closer to a coin-flip than a comfortable passage. From there the odds thin quickly: 7.1% to reach the last 16, under 1% to make a quarter-final, and effectively no path to the title. A defensible, hard-to-beat outsider, not a contender.

Algeria.text:
Algeria arrive in good shape, ranked 28th in the world and carrying a recent run that catches the eye: a 1-0 win away to the Netherlands in June, a goalless draw with Uruguay and a 7-0 demolition of Guatemala all came inside the last three friendly windows. The Africa Cup of Nations campaign was more mixed — wins over Sudan, Burkina Faso, Equatorial Guinea and Congo DR, but a 2-0 loss to Nigeria. A €256.9m squad, fronted by defenders like Aït-Nouri and Bensebaïni, looks comfortably solid rather than spectacular.

The model reads that profile cautiously. It makes Algeria heavy favourites to clear the group stage at 84.6% to reach the round of 32, but the odds thin fast after that: 30.5% to reach the last 16, 14.9% to make a quarter-final, and just 6.2% to see a semi. Winning the group is only a 15.2% shot, which tells you the simulations expect a tight, competitive section. The deep-run numbers — 2.3% to reach the final, 0.7% to lift the trophy — frame this as a side likely to advance, but not one the model rates as a genuine contender.

Ghana.text:
Ghana arrive ranked 74th in the world, the lowest-rated side in a squad worth a respectable €234.6m, and the contrast between their two recent lives tells the story. In World Cup qualifying the Black Stars were tidy and efficient — wins over Comoros, Mali and a 5-0 dismantling of the Central African Republic, with only a 1-1 draw away to Chad blotting the run. Against stronger opposition in friendlies, though, the floor fell out: 0-2 to Japan, 0-1 to South Korea, 1-5 to Austria, 1-2 to Germany and 0-2 to Mexico, before a 1-1 draw with Wales steadied things. That is one win in their last six against non-African teams.

The model reads that split cautiously. It gives Ghana a 47.4% chance of clearing the group into the round of 32 — essentially a coin flip — but only 9.75% to reach the last 16 and 2% to make the quarter-finals. Winning the group is priced at just 3.69%, and the deeper runs barely register, with the title a rounding-error 0.01%. A team that beats its peers but folds against the elite has a clear ceiling here.

Cape Verde.text:
Cape Verde arrive at their first World Cup as a side that earned the trip the hard way, ranked 69th in the world and worth a modest €54.5m. The qualifying run did the heavy lifting: a 1-0 home win over Cameroon, a 2-0 victory in Mauritius and a 3-0 dismantling of Eswatini, with only a 3-3 draw in Libya blotting the campaign. The warm-up form has been encouraging too — back-to-back 3-0 friendly wins over Serbia and Bermuda, and a 1-1 draw with Finland — though a 4-2 defeat in Chile is a reminder of the step up in class.

The model is blunt about where that leaves the Tubarões Azuis. It gives them a 31% chance of surviving the group stage into the round of 32, but only 4.2% of reaching the last 16 and 0.9% of a quarter-final. Winning the group is priced at just 1.4%, and the title at effectively zero. In short, this is a tournament about the experience and the occasion; clearing one knockout hurdle would already count as a genuine overachievement for a debutant nation.

Curaçao.text:
The numbers that matter for Curaçao start with how they got here. Their CONCACAF qualifying run was unbeaten across the stretch in our records: a 7-0 demolition of Bermuda, a 2-0 home win over Jamaica, plus draws away to Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago that did the quiet work. Ranked 82nd in the world with a squad valued at €25.78m — modest by tournament standards — this is a side built on organisation rather than star power, with three goalkeepers and a defensive spine led by Bazoer and Brenet headlining the named group.

The friendlies since tell a harder story. Heavy defeats away to Australia (1-5), China (0-2) and Scotland (1-4) suggest the step up against ranked opposition is steep, even after a 4-0 send-off against Aruba. The model reads it cautiously: just an 8.1% chance of reaching the round of 32, 0.83% to make the last 16, and barely 0.49% to win the group. Simply being here is the achievement; the simulations treat anything beyond the group stage as a long shot worth watching rather than backing.

Haiti.text:
Haiti arrive ranked 83rd in the world with a squad valued at just €55.9m, and the model treats them as long-shots: a 24.6% chance to clear the round of 32, dropping to 4.7% for the round of 16 and only 1.4% to win their group. The route effectively ends there — quarter-final odds of 0.9% and a championship probability rounded to zero tell you where the simulations place a side this size. This is a tournament about survival, not silverware.

The qualifying form, though, suggests they belong. Haiti held Honduras to a 0-0 draw, edged Costa Rica 1-0, beat Nicaragua home and away and traded a wild 3-3 in San José, the only real blemish a 0-3 loss in Honduras. Recent friendlies have been mixed — a 4-0 thumping of New Zealand alongside narrow defeats to Peru and Tunisia and a 1-1 with Iceland — so the goalkeeping depth of Duverger, Pierre and Placide and a back line built around Ade and Duverne will be tested. Getting out of the group would beat the numbers, but the qualifying results say it is no fantasy.

Iraq.text:
Iraq reach the World Cup as one of its lower-ranked sides, 57th by FIFA and carrying a squad valued at just €21.2m, but the Lions of Mesopotamia arrive on a respectable run. They edged Bolivia 1-0 — sorry, 2-1 — in the intercontinental play-off in April, beat the UAE 2-1 in Asian qualifying, and then held Spain to a 1-1 draw in a June friendly, the kind of result that suggests this is a hard team to break down rather than one that overwhelms anyone. The 0-0 away to Saudi Arabia and the tight wins fit a profile built on defensive organisation, with three goalkeepers and five defenders headlining the named squad.

The model treats that ceiling honestly. It gives Iraq a 13.3% chance of escaping the group into the round of 32 and just 2.3% of reaching the round of 16, with winning the group a remote 0.96% and a quarter-final almost off the table at 0.34%. In plain terms, the numbers see a competitive, awkward opponent who can nick results but is most likely heading home after three matches.

H. Kane.text:
Kane's club output hasn't tailed off with age — it's accelerated. In 2024 he managed 26 Bundesliga goals in 31 appearances at a 7.7 rating; the following campaign he pushed that to 36 in the same 31 games, lifting his rating to 7.87 and adding 14 in 13 Champions League outings at a remarkable 8.0. Throw in 10 DFB Pokal goals from six matches and this is a striker scoring at better than a goal a game across competitions, not coasting on reputation at 32.

That form has carried straight into international duty: two goals in two World Cup qualifiers this season, plus another in a friendly, with an 8.1 qualifying rating. For a player who scored eight in eight European qualifiers in the prior cycle, the conversion is relentless and the trajectory is still pointing up. England's tournament hopes lean heavily on him, and the underlying numbers suggest that reliance is well placed rather than a gamble on a fading talisman.

J. David.text:
Jonathan David arrives at the tournament with a club profile that splits neatly in two. The 2024 season was his peak: 16 Ligue 1 goals in 32 games for Lille at a 7.15 rating, plus a sharp Champions League return. The move to Juventus flattened that line. Across 35 Serie A appearances in 2025 he managed just 6 goals at a 6.43 rating, his lowest figure on this page, with another lean Champions League run at 6.30. That is a striker getting fewer minutes per goal and finishing colder in a tighter system.

The reassuring counterweight is Canada. David has scored in nearly every red-shirt window listed — two in Copa America, two in friendlies, two more in Nations League at a 7.53 rating — and he opens 2026 with 2 goals in 4 friendlies. The club dip is real and worth respecting, but his international output has held steady regardless of club form, which is what matters most here.

Mikel Oyarzabal.text:
Oyarzabal's club output is trending the right way at exactly the right time. His La Liga numbers jumped from nine goals in 2,262 minutes across 2024 to 15 in 2,714 minutes through 2025, with his league rating climbing from 6.79 to 7.08 — a striker scoring more often and contributing more across the board. The cup work backs it up: four goals and four assists in just four 2024 Copa del Rey ties at an 8.28 rating shows he sharpens in knockout football, the format that decides a World Cup.

For Spain, the case is even stronger. He hit six goals and four assists in six European qualifiers at 7.88, then opened 2026 with two goals in two friendlies off 63 minutes and an 8.7 rating. That is a player finishing chances at a rate well above his career baseline. Behind a top-ranked side, the 28-year-old projects as a reliable scorer rather than a peripheral squad option — a genuine asset for a deep run.

Kylian Mbappé.text:
Mbappé arrived at Real Madrid and scored at a rate that flatters even his reputation: 31 La Liga goals in 34 games across the 2024 campaign, then 25 in 31 the following season, with the Champions League return jumping from seven in 14 to a remarkable 15 in 11. That's a striker whose output didn't dip after a club move but climbed, and who saves his best for the biggest stages — an 8.05 Champions League rating in 2025 is elite.

For France, the signal is just as loud. In World Cup qualifying he posted five goals and three assists in four matches at an 8.38 rating, the highest figure on this page. Wearing the armband for the world's top-ranked side, he is the obvious focal point of their tournament hopes. The only caution is volume of recent international evidence: just four friendlies in 2026, 219 minutes, one goal at a quieter 7.03. On club form, though, few forwards enter the World Cup carrying more weight of expectation, and deservedly so.

Lautaro Martínez.text: A note of honesty up front: the data attached to this page belongs to Emiliano Martínez, Argentina's goalkeeper, not to Lautaro Martínez, so there is nothing here on the striker's club form and we won't invent it. What the dossier actually describes is a 33-year-old keeper whose numbers have drifted down rather than up. At Aston Villa his Premier League rating slipped from 7.09 across 3,196 minutes in 2024 to 6.98 over 2,835 minutes in 2025, and his European work cooled too, from a strong 7.42 in the Champions League to 7.12 in the Europa League. The 2026 sample is thinner and softer still: a 6.93 rating across 16 World Cup qualifiers and just 51 friendly minutes. Read straight, that is a reliable but no longer ascending performer heading into the tournament with third-ranked Argentina. Until the page is corrected, treat any Lautaro-specific read here as unsupported.

E. Haaland.text:
Haaland's club output reads like a metronome. In the 2024 Premier League season he scored 22 in 32 appearances at a 7.25 rating; in 2025 he pushed that to 27 goals and eight assists across 35 games, his rating ticking up to 7.31. The Champions League tells the same story — eight goals in each campaign — so there is no sign of decline heading into the tournament at age 25.

The international number that jumps out is even louder: 16 goals in eight World Cup qualifying matches across 2024, plus seven in six Nations League outings. That is a striker who scales up, not down, in a Norway shirt. The caveat is the most recent sample — two goals in two 2026 qualifiers, but then two friendlies with no goals and a flat 6.5 rating. Against that, Norway sit only 31st in FIFA's ranking, so much of their ceiling rests on whether Haaland's club-level scoring rate travels. On this evidence, it usually does.

Cristiano Ronaldo.text:
At 40, Ronaldo's club output hasn't dipped — if anything it's climbed. He scored 25 Pro League goals in 30 games across 2024, then bettered it with 28 in 30 the following season, adding 14 in 16 King's Cup ties along the way. That's a striker still finishing at better than a goal a game in his domestic competition, with ratings hovering around 7.2 to 7.5. The international evidence is just as loud: 8 goals in 8 Nations League outings and 5 in 5 World Cup qualifiers point to a player Portugal can still build a tournament around, even ranked fifth in the world.

The caution is volume against quality. Much of that scoring comes in the Saudi Pro League and cup runs, not Champions League-level resistance, and his lone 2026 appearance so far was a quiet 45-minute friendly that earned a 6.5. The goals are real, but expect them weighted toward Portugal's more open group games rather than the tightest knockout nights.

R. Jiménez.text: Jiménez's club trajectory points one way: gently downward. His 2024 at Fulham was his peak, 12 Premier League goals across 38 games at a 7.01 rating, a genuine focal-point season for a then-33-year-old. The 2025 campaign softened that — nine goals in 36 league outings and a rating dipping to 6.68 — which is the kind of slide you expect from a striker now 34 carrying heavy minutes. The international picture flatters him more: five goals in three Nations League games in 2024 at an 8.77 rating show he still punishes weaker CONCACAF defences, even if a single goal in three 2025 Gold Cup matches and a quiet start to 2026 (one goal in three friendlies, 6.90) temper that. For the tournament, read him as a dependable but no longer prolific lead line — capable against the group-stage opposition he tends to feast on, less likely to carry Mexico against the elite. The trend in his finishing matters as much as the totals.

L. Messi.text:
At 38, Messi's club output has gone up, not down. His 2024 MLS season brought 21 goals and 11 assists in 22 games at an 8.33 rating; in 2025 he pushed that to 35 goals and 23 assists across 31 league appearances, lifting his rating to 8.6. The 2026 campaign so far reads the same way — 13 goals and seven assists in 14 MLS outings, an 8.67 rating, even while nominally listed as a midfielder. That is not a player winding down, and it travels: across South American qualifying he scored eight in 12 with an 8.03 rating, the most reliable evidence of how this form holds against international defences rather than MLS ones.

For a side ranked third in the world, that combination of volume and creativity is the engine the model leans on. The one honest caveat is age and minutes management — light friendly cameos suggest careful handling — but on goals and assists per game, Messi is producing at the best rate of these three seasons.

Brahim Díaz.text:
At Real Madrid the story is a quiet decline in end product. In 2024 Brahim Díaz managed four goals and two assists across 1,405 La Liga minutes at a 6.86 rating; in 2025 his return fell to a single league goal, even as he turned creator with six assists, and his rating slipped to 6.68. His Champions League output cooled in step, two goals and a 7.01 rating in 2024 down to one goal and 6.79. So at club level he is drifting from scorer toward facilitator, often off the bench.

The international picture is the inversion. For Morocco he has been ruthless: seven goals in just 233 AFCON qualifying minutes at an 8.22 rating, then five more at the finals. That gap matters for the tournament. The club numbers say manage expectations on volume, but the national-team record suggests Morocco unlock a sharper, more direct Brahim than Madrid have lately, and his finishing in that shirt is the genuine edge.

M. Olise.text:
Olise has done nothing but climb since arriving at Bayern. His first Bundesliga season in 2024 produced 12 goals and 15 assists across 34 games at a 7.92 rating; his second went further still, 15 goals and 19 assists in 32 league outings at 7.89. The Champions League tells the same story — five goals in each campaign, and six assists in 2025 against two the year before — so this isn't a player flattered by a weak domestic league. At 24 he is sharpening, not plateauing.

For France, the early signs back that up. He carried his club rhythm into qualifying, where five appearances brought an 8.42 rating, and his four friendlies in 2026 have already yielded three goals and an assist at 7.83. Top-ranked France can lean on a creator who both scores and supplies in roughly equal measure, and on this trajectory Olise looks like a genuine tournament difference-maker rather than a rotation option.

F. Wirtz.text:
Wirtz arrives in different shape than the prodigy who tore up the Bundesliga. In his final 2024 Leverkusen campaign he posted 10 goals and 12 assists across 31 league games at a 7.70 rating, with another six goals in the Champions League. The 2025 move to Liverpool flattened that output: 33 Premier League appearances yielded just five goals and three assists, and his rating slid to 6.81 — a clear step down from the numbers that made his name. The Champions League work was steadier at 7.19, but the headline drop is real and worth weighing against the hype.

What tips the read back toward optimism is the Germany shirt. In four 2026 friendlies he has already produced three goals and two assists at a 7.95 rating, easily his sharpest recent form. At 22 he remains central to Germany's attack, and the international setting has consistently lifted him above his club ceiling — the most encouraging signal heading into the tournament.

B. Embolo.text:
Embolo's club output has quietly climbed. At Monaco across 2024 he managed six goals and four assists in 29 Ligue 1 appearances at a 6.75 rating, sharpening to a 6.98 mark over 750 Champions League minutes. The move to Rennes lifted the raw return: nine goals and three assists in 31 league games in 2025, even if the underlying rating held flat at 6.71. That's a striker scoring more without dominating matches — useful, not transcendent, at club level.

The international picture is brighter, and that matters more here. He hit four goals in six World Cup qualifiers at a 7.23 rating, added three in four friendlies through 2025, and has opened 2026 with two goals and a 7.27 rating in three more. The pattern is consistent: Embolo plays bigger for Switzerland than for his clubs. For a side ranked 19th leaning on him up front, that step-up in the national shirt is the number worth trusting into the tournament.

V. Gyökeres.text:
At Sporting CP in 2024 Gyökeres was a genuine phenomenon: 39 goals in 33 Primeira Liga matches at a 7.99 rating, with six more in the Champions League and a remarkable nine in six Nations League games for Sweden, where his rating hit 8.65. That is the profile of an elite penalty-box finisher.

The 2025 move to Arsenal tells a cooler story. Fourteen Premier League goals in 36 appearances is respectable output, but the rating slipped to 6.62, and his Champions League work (five in 13, rating 6.75) sat in the same modest band. The volume of chances and the easy dominance of Portugal did not fully translate to England.

For the tournament, that split matters. The model should lean on his international scoring, which has stayed strong regardless of club setting, while recognising that his year against top defences was solid rather than spectacular. With Sweden ranked 38th, Gyökeres is the swing factor: their ceiling rises or falls largely on which version turns up.

L. Díaz.text:
Díaz has trended sharply upward across the move from Merseyside to Munich. His final Liverpool campaign was productive without being prolific: 13 goals and 5 assists in 36 Premier League games at a 7.27 rating. The Bayern season reframes him entirely. In the Bundesliga he posted 15 goals and 14 assists across 32 matches, the kind of double-figure creation he'd never previously hit, and his Champions League rating of 7.52 from 12 appearances was his sharpest output anywhere. That is a player who has added a playmaking dimension to the running threat, and he's doing it nominally from midfield.

For the tournament, that breadth matters. Colombia leaned on him through qualifying, where he managed 7 goals and 3 assists in 17 games at a 7.25 rating, and at 28 he arrives in peak form rather than hoping to recapture it. A side ranked 13th in the world has its most in-form attacker firing on two fronts, which lifts both their ceiling and his individual scoring odds.

S. Mané.text:
At 33, Sadio Mané remains the engine of Senegal's attack, and his club output suggests the legs are still there. His first Saudi season was his most productive: 14 goals and 11 assists in 32 Pro League games at a 7.56 rating, comfortably his best figures in the dossier. The 2025 campaign reads slightly cooler — 10 goals and six assists in 25 league appearances at 7.28 — but the dip coincides with a move deeper into midfield, where the goals naturally thin while the creation stays. That positional shift carried into Senegal duty: at the Africa Cup of Nations he played as a midfielder and still returned two goals and three assists in seven games.

The early 2026 signal is loud, if tiny — two goals in a single 60-minute friendly, rated 8.9. One match settles nothing, but a player still scoring freely at international level, ranked 14th in the world, is exactly the kind of carry-the-team profile that travels into a tournament.

Raphinha.text:
Raphinha arrives off the back of a 2024 that reads like a peak season: 18 La Liga goals and nine assists, then a remarkable 13 goals and eight assists in just 14 Champions League outings at an 8.25 rating. That is elite-level output, and it sets the bar he is being measured against.

The 2025 numbers cool the story slightly. Reinvented as a midfielder, he still scored 13 in 22 La Liga games, but the rating slipped to 7.55 and the Champions League return fell to three goals in seven. The shape of his game changed more than its quality collapsed.

For Brazil, the deeper role has carried over. Across 13 World Cup qualifiers he chipped in five goals and two assists at a steady 7.42, though three recent friendlies brought no goals and a flatter 6.6. With Brazil sixth in the FIFA ranking, Raphinha looks more creative hub than out-and-out finisher now — productive, but no longer the runaway scorer of 2024.

Vinícius Júnior.text:
At club level, Vinícius has been relentlessly productive. His 2024 split 11 La Liga goals and eight assists across 30 games at a 7.37 rating, then went up a gear in front of goal in Champions League nights with eight strikes in 12. The 2025 league campaign was sharper still: 16 goals in 36 outings at 7.51, his best return here, even if the assists thinned out to five. The Champions League work turned more creative, a balanced five goals and five assists.

The caution is what happens in a Brazil shirt. South American qualifying tells a different story — just two goals and one assist in 11 appearances, often deployed in midfield, at a flat 6.93 rating that sits well below his Madrid baseline. Recent friendlies (7.27) hint the edge is still there, but the gap between his club ceiling and his national-team output is the number to watch. The talent guarantees little for the tournament; converting it for Brazil is the open question.

K. De Bruyne.text:
The headline number with De Bruyne is the move and what it has and hasn't cost him. His final Manchester City Premier League season in 2024 brought 4 goals and 7 assists across 33 games at a 7.32 rating, solid creative output if a step down from his peak. The 2025 switch to Napoli has, if anything, sharpened his goalscoring: 5 goals in 18 Serie A appearances, though the assist count has thinned to 2 and the rating dipped slightly to 7.04. At 34, that profile reads as a still-productive operator rather than a dominant one.

For the tournament, the more compelling evidence sits in a Belgium shirt. His World Cup qualifying return of 6 goals and 1 assist in 6 games at an 8.27 rating is exceptional, and a 7.33 rating across four 2026 friendlies suggests he arrives in rhythm. For a ninth-ranked side, De Bruyne remains the creative pivot the model leans on.

Son Heung-Min.text:
Son's club output has zig-zagged. His final Tottenham season in 2024 was steady rather than explosive — seven Premier League goals and nine assists at a 7.26 rating — before the move to Los Angeles FC sparked a scoring burst, 12 goals in just 11 MLS appearances and an 8.18 rating across the back half of 2025. The 2026 club picture is stranger: zero goals in 13 MLS games, though eight assists and a 7.15 rating say the creativity hasn't gone anywhere, and another six assists in CONCACAF Champions League. The goal drought reads as a shift toward provider rather than finisher at 33.

For the tournament, the number that matters most is what he does in a Korea shirt. Seven goals and four assists in 13 World Cup qualifiers at a 7.81 rating is elite international form, well clear of his recent club scoring. The finishing tap, in other words, still turns on for South Korea — which is exactly what their summer hinges on.

Bruno Fernandes.text:
Fernandes arrives at 31 with no sign of decline. His 2024-25 Premier League line — 9 goals and 21 assists across 35 games at a 7.63 rating — is the standout, the assist tally more than doubling the 10 he managed the season before on near-identical minutes. That points to a player whose creative output is rising, not fading, even as the goals stay steady around 8-9 a league campaign. He also showed he travels: a 7-goal, 4-assist Europa League run at an 8.05 rating is exactly the kind of knockout-football return a deep tournament rewards.

For Portugal, ranked fifth in the world, the implication is straightforward. Fernandes is a volume creator who keeps his rating in the high 7s whatever the competition, and the early 2026 friendlies (a goal and an assist in three caps) suggest he's ticking over fine. The model will treat him as Portugal's primary assist engine, and on this evidence that's a sound read rather than a hopeful one.

S. Rahimi.text:
Rahimi's club output has cooled markedly across two seasons. In 2024 he was a genuine threat for Al Ain, scoring eight in 18 Pro League games at a 7.44 rating and adding five in just seven AFC Champions League Elite outings at 7.54. The 2025 campaign told a different story: two league goals in 15 appearances, his rating down to 6.98, and a blank across three FIFA Club World Cup games at 6.85. The 2026 friendlies have continued that trend, one goal in four with a 6.68 rating.

The complication is that his international ceiling has stayed high even as the club numbers sagged — five goals in three Africa Cup of Nations games, plus three goals and two assists in qualifying. So the read is genuinely split: a player whose week-to-week club form points downward but who keeps finding the net for Morocco. For a tournament, that makes him a streaky bet rather than a banker, capable of a hot run but no longer scoring at his 2024 rate.

C. Gakpo.text:
Gakpo's club trajectory has flattened just as the tournament approaches. His 2024 Liverpool season was his sharpest: 10 Premier League goals and four assists in 35 games at a 7.22 rating, with ruthless cup returns on top (five goals in six League Cup outings). The 2025 campaign tells a quieter story — seven league goals and five assists across 36 matches, but the rating slipped to 6.89 as he was used more as a midfielder than an out-and-out attacker, and his ceiling shows: zero goals in seven FA Cup and Champions League appearances early on.

The encouraging signal is that he raises his game in orange. He was lethal in World Cup qualifying for the seventh-ranked Dutch (four goals, four assists, an 8.06 rating), and his 2026 friendly form holds up at 7.85 with two goals in four. The club dip tempers expectations, but his international record argues he turns up when it matters most.

M. Taremi.text:
Taremi's last two years tell a clear story of a player who needed minutes and found them. At Inter in 2024 he was a fringe figure, just 816 Serie A minutes across 26 appearances for a single league goal, though his Champions League numbers were healthier at a 7.08 rating with a goal and three assists in 714 minutes. The 2025 move to Olympiakos restored him: 10 goals and a 7.07 rating in 1,261 Super League minutes, plus two more in the Champions League. That rhythm has carried into international football, where his World Cup qualifying return of five goals and four assists in 15 games, at a standout 7.76 rating, is comfortably his best work in this dossier.

For the tournament, the read is encouraging. At 33 he is playing regularly and scoring, and an Iran forward delivering a near-goal-involvement-a-game in qualifying is exactly the profile you want leading the line. The Inter slump looks like a usage problem, not a decline.

A. Ueda.text:
Ueda's club trajectory points one way: up. In 2024 he managed seven Eredivisie goals from 21 appearances at a 6.83 rating, useful but unremarkable. The 2025 season was a different player entirely — 25 league goals in 31 games, 2,533 minutes and a 7.17 rating, the kind of season that turns a squad striker into a focal point. He carried that into 2026 World Cup qualifying, where he scored eight times in nine matches at a 7.49 rating, the best number on his page.

The caveat is the step up in level. Outside the Eredivisie his returns thin out — one goal in six Europa League games, blanks in limited Champions League minutes — and three recent Japan friendlies brought no goals at a 6.37 rating. So the profile is a striker in genuinely hot domestic and qualifying form whose ceiling against the tournament's best is still unproven. For a Japan side ranked 18th, that finishing run makes him a real threat; the open question is whether it travels.

Lamine Yamal.text:
At 18, Lamine Yamal's trajectory points one way: up. His 2024 La Liga return of 9 goals and 13 assists at a 7.79 rating was the work of a precocious creator; his 2025 league line — 16 goals and 11 assists across 2,268 minutes, rating up to 7.95 — is that of a finished one, with the goal output nearly doubling. The Champions League tells the same story, his 8.14 rating there in 2025 his highest in any major competition, alongside 6 goals and 4 assists in ten games. A nominal shift from attacker to midfielder hasn't dulled the numbers; if anything it has broadened them.

The caveat is small but worth flagging: his only 2026 sample is two Spain friendlies, 108 minutes, no goals or assists and a modest 7.1. That's far too little to read into. For a side ranked second in the world, a forward arriving in this kind of two-season ascent is exactly the profile that wins knockout games.

Pedri.text:
Pedri arrives as a metronome rather than a goalscorer, and the numbers say as much. His 2024 La Liga campaign was his most complete in recent memory — 36 appearances, 2,808 minutes, four goals and five assists at a 7.62 rating — and he carried that into Spain duty, where his World Cup qualifying rating spiked to a standout 8.50 across four games with two goals. The 2025 season reshaped his output: the goals dried up to two, but the creation surged to nine assists in La Liga at a near-identical 7.54 rating, marking him out as a chance-maker more than a finisher.

The caution is recent. Across three 2026 friendlies he has logged just 90 minutes total at a 7.10 rating, so his sharpness heading into the tournament is the open question rather than his quality. For the world's second-ranked side, a fit Pedri at his 2024 European-qualifying level is a genuine tournament swing factor; a half-loaded one is a more modest bet.

Vitinha.text:
A model in metronomic form. Across two PSG seasons Vitinha has barely dipped below a 7.5 match rating, and the underlying numbers have only sharpened. His 2024 was the steady-anchor version — 5 goals in 2,035 Ligue 1 minutes, a 7.56 in the Champions League — but 2025 is where his game widened. He turned into a creator domestically, laying on 7 assists in 29 league games at a 7.58 rating, then a goal threat in Europe with 6 strikes across 17 Champions League outings, again at 7.58. That blend of control and end product, from a 25-year-old central midfielder, is exactly what a fifth-ranked Portugal wants pulling the strings.

The caveat for the tournament is sample size on the international side: just 88 minutes across two friendlies in 2026, no goals or assists. But his Portugal body of work is real — three Nations League assists and a 7.68 in World Cup qualifying. The club evidence says he arrives in peak rhythm.

Ousmane Dembélé.text:
Dembélé's club trajectory tells a clear story. The 2024 campaign was the peak: 21 goals and seven assists in 30 Ligue 1 games at a 7.72 rating, with another eight goals and six assists in the Champions League. The 2025 numbers cooled but stayed strong — 10 goals and seven assists in 22 league outings (7.41), and again eight goals in Europe, though the assist count there dropped to two. Either way, this is a forward who scores at volume across the hardest competition on the continent, which matters for a France side ranked number one in the world.

The flag is recent and positional. His only 2026 minutes come in two France friendlies, 120 minutes at a 6.95 rating with no goals and a single assist, deployed as a midfielder rather than an attacker. We've seen this before — France used him deeper at the Euros too. If he plays as a true attacker in the summer, the goal model likes him; pushed into midfield, his output expectation should be trimmed.

Rayan Cherki.text:
At 22, Rayan Cherki has spent two seasons climbing without dropping off. His 2024 at Lyon was the breakout: 8 goals and 11 assists in 30 Ligue 1 games at a 7.63 rating, plus a glittering 4 goals and 8 assists in the Europa League where his 8.02 rating outshone everything else he did that year. The 2025 move to Manchester City could have stalled him; instead the creative output held up. He managed only 4 goals in 33 Premier League appearances but added 12 assists, with a 7.20 rating and useful cup returns — three goals in the League Cup, three in the Champions League.

The pattern is consistent: a midfielder who manufactures more chances than he finishes, and who has done it in a tougher league without regressing. For the top-ranked France, that points to a high-floor supporting creator rather than a primary goalscorer. His three 2026 friendlies (one goal, 7.27) are too few to read much into either way.

Jude Bellingham.text:
Bellingham's club trajectory tells a story of a debut-season peak and a quieter follow-up. His first Real Madrid campaign in 2024 returned 9 goals and 8 assists across 31 La Liga games at a 7.48 rating, with a further 3 goals and 3 assists in the Champions League. The 2025 numbers cooled: 6 goals and 4 assists in 28 league outings at 7.28, and a 7.2 rating across nine European nights. The output dropped, even if the floor stayed high.

What lifts the read for the tournament is the England version of him. He scored and created at the Euros (7.44) and was outstanding in the Nations League, rating 8.33 while deployed as an attacker rather than a deeper midfielder. His early 2026 work is thin but tidy — an assist and a 7.6 in World Cup qualifying. At 22 and ranked behind a fourth-placed side, he profiles as a player whose club returns understate his international ceiling, particularly when pushed higher up the pitch.

Unai Simón.text:
Unai Simón arrives as a settled, heavily-used number one rather than a question mark. Across 2025 he was Athletic Club's workhorse, playing 37 La Liga matches for 3,330 minutes at a 6.88 rating, with another eight Champions League outings at a slightly thinner 6.50. The previous season carried more polish — a 7.09 La Liga mark and, more tellingly, a 7.22 across six Euro 2024 games for Spain, the kind of major-tournament return that travels well. The blemishes are isolated rather than structural: a 4.60 in the 2025 Super Cup stands out precisely because nothing around it does.

For a Spain side ranked second in the world, that profile reads as dependable continuity. His two 2026 friendly appearances landed at 7.30, a small but encouraging signal that he is arriving in form. There is no rotation drama and no stylistic surprise here — just a goalkeeper with proven international ceiling and an iron-man club season behind him, which is broadly what a contender wants from its last line.

J. Pickford.text:
